cards.title: Introduction to Controllers
cards.content:
Controllers are the heart of the handling requests in ASP.NET Core MVC and Web API applications.

They inherit from Controller (for views) or ControllerBase (for APIs) and contain public methods known as Action Methods.

cards.title: Routing and Attributes
cards.content:
ASP.NET Core uses attribute routing to map URLs to controller actions.

[Route("api/[controller]")]
[ApiController]
public class ProductsController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet]
    public IActionResult Get() => Ok(new string[] { "A", "B" });
}

cards.title: Fill in the Routing Token
cards.content: To automatically substitute the controller name in the route attribute, use the [Route("api/_{blank}_")] token.

cards.title: Action Results
cards.content:
Action methods can return primitive types, complex types, or implementation of IActionResult.

Helper methods like Ok(), NotFound(), and BadRequest() make returning standard HTTP status codes easy.

content.instructions: Match the HTTP status code helper to its corresponding code.
Order the steps of an incoming HTTP request handling in ASP.NET Core Web API.

items.text: HTTP Request arrives at the server
Routing middleware selects the appropriate Controller and Action
Action method executes and returns IActionResult
HTTP Response is sent back to the client

cards.title: Model Binding and Validation
cards.content:
ASP.NET Core automatically maps incoming HTTP request data to action method parameters using Model Binding.

You can validate the model using ModelState.IsValid inside your controller action.

cards.title: Summary
cards.content: You have learned the fundamentals of ASP.NET Core Controllers, including routing, action results, model binding, and HTTP status codes.
